claims.text: Elevated-temperature service exposure transforms the metastable Mg-containing high-entropy alloy.
Nanoscale intermetallic precursor phases nucleate preferentially at grain boundaries and defects.
Early segregation can evolve into a homogeneous, fine-scale intermetallic dispersion.
Early segregation can instead evolve into coarse, continuous intermetallic networks.
A fine-scale intermetallic dispersion retains protective corrosion properties.
A fine-scale intermetallic dispersion retains protective high-temperature oxidation properties.
Coarse, continuous intermetallic networks undermine surface passivation.
Mg and other species diffuse from the matrix to defect sites during transformation.
At 400–500 °C, diffusion kinetics favor a fine dispersion of intermetallic precipitates.
Fine intermetallic precipitates help maintain a stable protective oxide scale.
Above 500 °C, faster diffusion produces coarser and more interconnected intermetallic networks.
Coarse interconnected intermetallic networks disrupt passive-film integrity.
Disruption of passive-film integrity reduces corrosion resistance.
Disruption associated with coarse intermetallic networks reduces high-temperature oxidation resistance.
Lower-temperature-aged samples will retain corrosion and oxidation resistance relative to the initial metastable state.
Higher-temperature-aged samples will exhibit a measurable loss of corrosion and oxidation resistance relative to the initial metastable state.
A critical threshold near 500 °C governs the transition from fine-scale to coarse-scale intermetallic evolution.

contradictions.description: The conditions and predictions include a lower regime of 400–500 °C, but the boundary says the hypothesis applies within or above a roughly 500 °C threshold, potentially excluding the below-threshold portion of that lower regime.
